query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In near‐equiatomic high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, the intrinsic high configurational entropy combined with significant lattice distortion creates sluggish diffusion kinetics that suppress phase separation and chemical segregation at elevated service temperatures, thereby preserving the single‐phase structure required for stable catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced by physical or chemical fabrication methods that exhibit a homogeneous single-phase distribution with random elemental arrangement.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal pre-annealing step (e.g., at ~700 K in an inert atmosphere) to modify the diffusion kinetics prior to exposure to the target operational temperatures, contrasting with nanoparticles that receive no pre-annealing.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under inert atmosphere with service temperature regimes of 773–1173 K for catalytic applications and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics. All nanoparticles should have identical size distributions and compositions to isolate the effect of pre-annealing.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion arising from atomic size differences in a high configurational entropy matrix, which acts as an energy barrier to atomic mobility.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes the single-phase solid solution, while the associated lattice distortion creates high energy barriers that slow down atomic diffusion. This sluggish diffusion prevents phase separation and elemental segregation even after prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures, maintaining the active and uniform surface necessary for catalytic and thermoelectric functionality.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles that undergo controlled pre-annealing will exhibit minimal changes in phase composition and chemical homogeneity after high-temperature exposure, whereas control nanoparticles without pre-treatment (or with enhanced atomic mobility) are likely to show signs of phase segregation or precipitation.
generation.baseline: As-synthesized nanoparticles without any pre-conditioning treatment, which may begin to show a modest degree of phase segregation and elemental redistribution under prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic, homogeneous solid-solution nanoparticles under inert reaction conditions. It may not hold for alloys with strong element-specific segregation tendencies or in oxidizing environments where additional surface reactions dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative values for the activation energies of diffusion in nanoparticles and the long-term stability thresholds remain uncertain, necessitating systematic experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with identical composition and size distributions. Subject one set to a pre-annealing treatment at 700 K for a predetermined time in an inert atmosphere, while keeping the other set as-synthesized. Then expose both sets to a prolonged thermal treatment at 900 K (within the catalytic operation regime) for a fixed duration. Periodically characterize both sets using high-resolution X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to monitor phase composition, elemental distribution, and any onset of segregation or secondary phase formation.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification via XRD
Elemental mapping and morphology via TEM/EDS
Surface composition and oxidation state via XPS
Particle size distribution consistency via electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the pre-annealed and as-synthesized nanoparticle sets exhibit similar levels of phase separation, elemental segregation, or formation of secondary phases after high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion preserve stability is falsified.

System: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V.
